name: Conversion — agent-run customer data conversions for vertical SaaS implementation teams
one_liner: For the implementation / onboarding lead at a 20-300 person vertical SaaS vendor (dental, veterinary, legal, field service, pediatric EHR), Conversion is a per-customer data conversion agent: it takes whatever the prospect's old system coughs up — a DB dump, a pile of CSVs, or PDF/printed reports — infers the undocumented codes, maps them into the vendor's own schema, loads through the vendor's API, and produces a reconciliation pack (record counts, financial control totals, exception list) the customer signs off on before go-live.
problem: Vertical SaaS vendors win a deal and then have to move the new customer off a legacy practice-management / field-service system before go-live. The legacy vendor often won't give a clean export: public switching guides warn that "we give you a PDF" is a red flag, documents come out as per-record requests, and some incumbents charge export fees (one operator publicly described a $70,000 export fee as a "hostage situation"). The receiving vendor absorbs the work. Open Dental publishes a retail conversion fee of $1,450 per database plus $850 for scanned docs and $900 for X-rays; IDEXX Neo lists $590; independent consultants quote $6,500-$15,000 for a standard migration and $18,000-$40,000 for complex ones. PCC documents a clinical conversion *queue* whose wait depends on queue length and can run several weeks. Vendors staff this with dedicated people — live postings include Practice Migration Specialist ($50-70k), Data Conversion Specialist ($75-125k), Senior Data Conversion Engineer ($105-130k). Today each conversion is a hand-built script plus a spreadsheet of code mappings plus a manual eyeball check, rebuilt per source system, and the conversion queue caps how many customers a vendor can onboard per month.
target_customer: The VP Implementation / Director of Onboarding (sometimes the CTO at smaller vendors) at a B2B vertical SaaS company doing roughly 5-50 customer conversions a year off named legacy competitors. Sweet spot: $5M-$50M ARR, 20-300 employees, 1-6 people on conversions. They own the professional-services P&L and the go-live date, so they own the budget. Secondary buyer: the specialist conversion shops and "we migrate your practice" agencies (WeMigrate-style) who would use it as a production tool.
why_now: Three things changed in the last year. (1) Computer-use / browser agents are now usable in production for driving legacy apps that have no API — Microsoft made computer use in Copilot Studio generally available in 2026 and Shield publicly describes running thousands of GPT-6-Astra legacy-portal runs a month — so the "there is no export" case is now attackable rather than impossible. (2) Document parsing with per-field confidence and citations (Reducto, Extend) got good enough to turn a printed legacy report into typed rows with evidence, which is exactly what a reconciliation pack needs. (3) Investors are pointing straight at this: a16z's [latest] Big Ideas 2026 "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) names PDFs/screenshots/semi-structured exports as the enterprise bottleneck, and "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (Joe Schmidt, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/) describes exactly the implementation-labour wedge. The bookmarked Auctor fireside (https://x.com/ycombinator/status/2122713026231238914) shows the same thesis being funded one layer up the stack: Sequoia-backed, $20M, selling to the people who *implement* enterprise software rather than to the end customer. Conversion sells to the same persona at the vertical-SaaS end, where no funded player is positioned.
comparables: Zengines (https://www.zengines.ai/) — AI data migration with "logic discovery" for undocumented legacy rules, explicitly markets customer onboarding for software companies; ~$14M raised per its own media kit, but positioned at enterprise financial services, sales-led with no public price. Gap: nothing packaged or priced for a vendor doing 5-50 conversions a year. Rocketlane Migration Agent (https://www.rocketlane.com/blogs/ai-data-migration) — migration playbooks, mapping and customer sign-off inside a PSA; custom-priced inside the Nitro Enterprise tier, and its published benchmarks skew to CRM-style sources. Gap: assumes you already bought the PSA, and assumes structured sources. Flatfile (https://flatfile.com/pricing/portal, Professional listed at $799/mo plus $2/file usage), OneSchema, Osmos, Dromo, Impler — embeddable importers for recurring customer-led CSV uploads. Gap: they start when you already have a clean file; they do not get the data out of a legacy desktop app, infer undocumented codes, or produce a sign-off pack. Reducto / Extend — excellent document parsing APIs with per-field confidence, but they are components, not a migration product: no report discovery, no cross-report reconciliation, no import connectors. WeMigrate (https://wemigrate.co.uk/systems/category/practice) and the per-vertical conversion shops — human services, fixed quote after scoping; they are the workaround buyers pay for today and a plausible first design partner. Open Dental's in-house conversion department (https://www.opendental.com/site/conversions.html) shows the incumbent answer: hire people and publish a price list.
market_note: Estimates, clearly labelled. A commercial directory lists ~3,800 vertical SaaS companies; call the realistic ICP a few thousand vendors worldwide doing meaningful conversion volume. Observed per-conversion economics give the pricing anchor: $590-$1,450 published retail for a simple practice conversion, $6.5k-$40k for consultant-run projects, and $6k-$12k of direct implementation labour per mid-market onboarding at 40-60 hours and $150-200/hr loaded (secondary benchmark, not audited). A vendor doing 30 conversions a year is spending roughly $100k-$300k of loaded labour on this; a $500-$1,500 per-conversion platform fee plus a small seat base is a 5-10x saving and a straightforward sell. 300 vendors at an average of 25 conversions a year at $800 is ~$6M ARR — a real but not enormous first market; expansion is into the conversion agencies and into the integration/ongoing-sync layer.
risks: 1) The work may be irreducibly bespoke: every legacy source has its own schema and its own undocumented codes, so the agent may only ever get to 70% and the last 30% still needs an engineer — which turns the product into a services business with software margins only after many repeats of the same source system. 2) The destination vendors may prefer to keep conversion in-house as a competitive weapon and a revenue line (Open Dental charges for it), making them reluctant to hand customer data to a third party. 3) Data sensitivity: dental/vet/legal/pediatric records mean BAAs, HIPAA and long security reviews for a one-person company — which is exactly why a self-hosted or runs-in-their-VPC first version may be necessary, slowing the first sale.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That a reusable source-system "recipe" exists — i.e. that the second Dentrix-to-X conversion is 5x cheaper than the first. If every conversion is unique, there is no software here. 2) That the implementation lead, not the CTO, can sign a $1-3k-per-conversion purchase without a six-month security review. 3) That the reconciliation pack (counts, control totals, exceptions, customer sign-off) is the part they actually value enough to pay for, rather than just the mapping — research found reconciliation tooling exists for enterprises but nothing packaged for implementation teams, which is suggestive, not proven.
first_customers: (a) Vertical SaaS vendors that publicly advertise "free migration from your old system" and therefore eat the cost themselves: NaVetor and Digitail (vet, naming AVImark/Cornerstone as sources), Vagaro (salon, "free transfer from any software"), Ascora (HVAC), Intellident (dental). Each of those marketing pages is a signed admission of the cost. (b) Vendors with a published conversion price list or a documented queue — Open Dental, IDEXX Neo, PCC, LEAP — where the pain already has a number on it. (c) The conversion agencies: WeMigrate, the independent practice-migration consultants quoting $6.5k-$15k per project. Find them via the "switching from <legacy system>" comparison pages every vertical SaaS vendor publishes, and via LinkedIn searches for "Data Conversion Specialist" / "Practice Migration Specialist" job postings — a live posting is a buying signal.
validation_test: This week: pick one vertical (dental or veterinary, where source systems are few and named). Get one real anonymised legacy export — ideally the ugly case, a set of printed/PDF reports — from a friendly practice or an agency. Run it through a hand-built pipeline and produce one artefact: a mapped import file plus a one-page reconciliation pack (patient count, open AR total, appointment count, 12 flagged exceptions with the source line cited). Then email 20 implementation leads at vendors from the list above with that single artefact and one question: "we did this conversion in 3 hours instead of 3 days — would you pay $1,000 per conversion for it?" Pass = 3 or more reply asking to try it on their own backlog, and at least 1 agrees to a paid pilot on a real customer within 30 days. Fail = replies are "interesting, we do this in-house" with no follow-up.
build_plan: Narrowest first version: one vertical, two named source systems, one destination vendor. Stack: TypeScript + Node, Postgres, a parsing API (Reducto or Extend) for PDF/report sources, a frontier model for code inference and mapping proposals, and the destination vendor's own REST API for loading. Steps: (1) Build the "source recipe" abstraction — a per-legacy-system definition of which reports/tables exist, how to read them, and the known code tables; ship recipes for exactly two sources. (2) Build the inference pass: given raw rows, propose a field map to the destination schema and flag every value whose meaning it cannot resolve, each with the source line cited. (3) Build the human review screen where the implementation consultant accepts/overrides mappings in bulk; every override is saved back into the recipe so the next conversion starts warmer. (4) Build the load: dry-run into the destination sandbox via API, then production, with rollback. (5) Build the reconciliation pack — record counts, financial control totals, orphan/duplicate list, 10 random spot-check records side by side, exported as a PDF the end customer signs. (6) Price per conversion, invoice the vendor. CUT for v1: computer-use extraction from live legacy desktop apps (ask for the export first; add the agent only once a recipe repeats), multi-tenant self-serve signup, any embeddable importer widget, imaging/X-ray binaries, ongoing sync, and anything resembling a PSA. Run the first five conversions forward-deployed, by hand where needed — the product is the recipe library that accumulates.
launch_post: Your new customer's old software only exports PDFs. So your implementation team spends three days rebuilding their data by hand. Conversion reads the reports, maps the fields, loads through your API, and hands the customer a signed reconciliation pack. Per conversion, not per seat.
reasoning:
Conversion won because it is the only candidate where I found both a named buyer with a published price for the manual workaround and a gap the funded players visibly decline to serve. The Auctor bookmark is the thesis in miniature: Sequoia paid up for a company that sells to the people who *implement* software rather than to the end user, because implementation labour is where the money leaks. Conversion applies that one layer down, to vertical SaaS vendors, at the single step that is both the most manual and the most dangerous — moving a new customer's history off a legacy system that may only export printed reports.

The evidence is unusually concrete for a first night on an idea: Open Dental publishes $1,450 per database plus $850 for scanned docs and $900 for X-rays; IDEXX Neo lists $590; independent consultants quote $6.5k-$40k; PCC documents a conversion *queue* measured in weeks; and there are live job postings for Practice Migration Specialist, Data Conversion Specialist and Senior Data Conversion Engineer at $50k-$130k. That is a role, a budget and a price, which is why pain and market_pull carry.

What keeps it at 7.2 rather than 8+: the wedge is genuinely months, not weeks. The product only becomes software — rather than a consultancy — if the second conversion off the same legacy system is dramatically cheaper than the first, and I could not verify that from outside; it is the riskiest assumption. Second, every published price I found is charged by the vendor *to the practice*, so vendor willingness to pay a third party is inferred. Third, the data is dental/vet/legal records, which means BAAs and security reviews that a solo builder on evenings and weekends will feel acutely — this is a "quit something" venture, not a side project, and the profile says that is the bar for a venture.

It is not a repeat of Asbuilt (2026-11-19). Asbuilt serves the delivery lead at a Dynamics/Acumatica *implementation partner* and extracts the as-built configuration of a tenant for documentation and handover. Conversion serves the implementation lead at a *software vendor* and moves an end customer's historical business data out of a third-party legacy product into the vendor's own schema, with a reconciliation and sign-off artefact. Different buyer, different direction of data flow, different deliverable.

Signals weighed: a16z [latest] "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" and "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" both aimed me at this, and both were used only to lift timing after I separately confirmed the parsing and computer-use capability actually shipped in 2026. YC's [latest] "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" were tested and rejected — the first as a library repeat, the second as a bad fit for this builder.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Conversion — agent-run customer data conversions for vertical SaaS implementation teams (from Auctor + a16z multimodal-data/forward-deployed signals). PICK. Named buyer, published prices for the workaround, a gap the importer vendors leave open at the ugly end.
2. Agent payroll/scope registry for finance teams running Grok-Bot-style accounting agents (from @bot). DROPPED — direct repeat of Shiftlog (2026-11-18) and Roster; same buyer, same core workflow.
3. Mid-market cash application agent for QuickBooks/Sage shops priced under HighRadius (from @bot). FINALIST → dropped at deep research. The category is saturated at every price point: HighRadius, Billtrust, Quadient AR/YayPay, Gaviti, Growfin, Stuut, Vero, Nuvo, Cashbook all sell exactly this to exactly this buyer, several explicitly positioned as "mid-market, cheaper than HighRadius". Gap would have scored 4.
4. Contract-to-invoice revenue assurance for B2B SaaS — audit billing config against signed terms (from @bot order-to-cash). DROPPED at screen. Research found only soft 1-5% leakage estimates with no mismatch-specific number, Safebooks and the revenue-assurance crowd already positioning on "validate contract-to-billing accuracy", and the buyer (RevOps) is a slow, political sale.
5. Hypercare triage copilot for system integrators post-go-live (from Auctor). FINALIST → dropped. Real pain, but Auctor itself is $20M-funded and moving down this exact corridor (sales → discovery → delivery), and the buyer is a consulting partner with long cycles. Too close to a funded incumbent's roadmap, and adjacent to Asbuilt already in the library.
6. Approval inbox for business-ops agents — one mobile queue for every agent's write that needs a human (from @digitalocean Cuttlefish + @bot). DROPPED at screen. Repeat-adjacent to Doublecheck/Ledger/Shiftlog, and the control plane is being absorbed by Auth0 CIBA, Copilot Studio, Zip, and the agent platforms themselves.
7. KYA / agent-identity onboarding for mid-market finance (a16z "from KYC to KYA" signal). DROPPED at screen. Baselayer raised $35M on exactly this, Okta and Experian shipped agent identity in 2026. Closed.
8. "Plaid for government benefits" wedge — document-proof reuse for one benefit program (YC [latest] signal, Gustaf Alströmer). DROPPED. Right-sized pain but wrong builder: public-sector procurement, 12-18 month cycles, no agent edge this builder can exercise on evenings and weekends; also no bookmark gave a way in.
9. AI for City Hall wedge — plan-check correction letters (YC [latest] signal). DROPPED as repeat: Backcheck (2026-10-28) is the same buyer and the same workflow.
10. WIP/unbilled recovery agent for small professional services firms (from the services-margin angle). DROPPED at screen. BigTime, Saviom, Rocketlane and every PSA already report unbilled WIP; the 10-20% unbilled statistic is vendor marketing and the buyer already owns a tool that shows it.
11. Legacy-report extraction API as a pure component (computer-use agents driving old desktop apps). DROPPED — merged into Conversion as its v2 capability. On its own it is a feature competing with Reducto/Extend, with no buyer of its own.

PROJECT
1. Houserules — paste your AGENTS.md, score it against a ~6,000-repo census, see the rules you're missing. PICK: the only candidate where a dataset published last month makes an evidence-backed personal verdict possible, and prior art (ossrules, agentlinter) was confirmed not to do it.
2. Agent payslip for the Grok Bot five — turn the x.ai order-to-cash bot roles into your own bot org chart. DROPPED at generation: near-identical to past ideas Roster (job title → team of bots) and Payslip. Repeat.
3. Clusterboard — a pretty local view of Apple container's new `container cluster` on macOS. DROPPED at screen: needs a local daemon (not a static page), audience is tiny, and Podman Desktop / Rancher / ClusterDeck already cover cluster visualisation.
4. Laundrygeo — browser-only geofenced reminders from trq212's laundry prompt. DROPPED at screen: the W3C geolocation issue (#214) confirms background geofencing is not available to web pages; it would be a PWA that only works while open. Dependency killed it.
5. Agentswitchboard — open-source console to see/approve agents running on a remote box (KlausCodes' ask, DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish). DROPPED at screen: a real expressed need, but a crowded field (Symphony, Open SWE, Cezar, 9+ orchestrators) and it is a 2-4 week backend build, not a weekend static page.
6. Untangled — paste a repo, get a messy-code map (duplication, wrapper-only files). DROPPED at screen: thin variation on a named bookmark (/untangle-codebase), and the builder's library already has Blindspot and Ghostwritten in the paste-a-repo lane.
7. Meetingartifact — turn a transcript into the doc/whiteboard Claude Meetings makes. DROPPED at screen: confirmed no public API for Claude Meetings artifacts, and it is a plain summariser with nothing to post.
8. SIP regret — "what if you'd started investing in 2019" shareable card, from the sipsea bookmark. DROPPED at screen: an enormous number of free SIP calculators exist in India; zero freshness, and the builder has no fintech data edge.
9. Smelltest — standalone linter for the six arXiv config smells. FINALIST, then folded into Houserules: on its own it duplicates agentlinter's job; the census comparison is what makes it new.
10. Rulebrowser — just a beautiful browsable shelf of 8,390 real AGENTS.md files. FINALIST, lost: lovely but passive, ossrules.md already curates something similar, and there is no personal input so nothing to post about yourself.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): summarised x.ai/news/grok-bot-accounting (five bots across order-to-cash; invoice issuance 24h→minutes, cash app 3-4h→~30min, all company-reported), the Auctor YC fireside subject (AI workspace for system integrators; $20M incl. Sequoia Series A, Apr 2026; buyers are SIs and professional-services firms, no public pricing), and DigitalOcean Cuttlefish (iPhone approval app for Managed Agents, Box as launch partner). Effect: the Grok post sent me toward order-to-cash, which deep research then killed as saturated; Auctor reframed the night around "sell to the implementers, not the end user", which is what produced the winner.

Screening pot (6 of 6): one search each on mid-market order-to-cash AI agents (found HighRadius, Billtrust, Quadient/YayPay, Gaviti, Growfin, Stuut, Vero, Nuvo — category closed); ERP implementation UAT/traceability (thin, mostly consultancies); KYA/agent identity (Baselayer $35M, Okta, Experian — closed); CAS/bookkeeping AI agents (Digits, Puzzle, Truewind already there); contract-to-billing revenue assurance (Safebooks positioning on the exact phrase); SI hypercare tooling (no product, but Auctor's own roadmap covers it). Four of six candidates died here, which is what the pot is for.

Deep research pot (12 of 12): spent entirely on Conversion and its two runners-up. Found the competitor set and prices (Flatfile $799/mo Professional + $2/file + $2.50/M values; Osmos reportedly ~$299/mo + per-record; Impler from ~$35/mo; OneSchema and Zengines quote-only; Zengines ~$14M raised per its own media kit; Rocketlane Migration Agent custom-priced inside Nitro Enterprise, platform base $49/user/mo with 5-seat minimum). Found the workaround prices (Open Dental $1,450/$850/$900 with volume discounts after the first three; IDEXX Neo $590; consultants $1.5-2.5k assessment, $6.5-15k standard, $18-40k complex; ezyVet scoped; DaySmart Vet free). Found the capacity evidence (PCC's documented clinical conversion queue; LEAP Transitions 5-7 working days; dental end-to-end 3-16 weeks; FieldRoutes import/cleanup occupying weeks 3-8 of a 2-3 month project). Found the role (four live postings, $50k-$130k). Found the ugly-source evidence (PDF-dump warnings in dental switching guides, per-patient document requests, a reported $70k export fee described as a hostage situation). Found the capability (Copilot Studio computer use GA in 2026; Shield running thousands of GPT-6-Astra legacy-portal runs/month; OSWorld-Verified 86% headline vs 61.5% on a hard IT-ticket set — enough to justify v2, not enough to build v1 on). Deliberately recorded what I could NOT verify: no per-conversion wholesale rate paid by vendors to shops, no quantified lost-deal evidence from migration friction, no credible count of vertical SaaS vendors beyond a 3,816-company commercial directory, and no practitioner consensus on which conversion stage eats the most labour. Those gaps are why gap and market_pull sit at 7 rather than 8.

Sharpening pot (2 of 5, both productive — I stopped because the third question I wanted answered, "do vendors pay third parties for this", returned nothing usable twice and I would rather report the uncertainty than pad the score): round 1 confirmed the reconciliation/sign-off gap for implementation teams, round 2 confirmed the buyer's published prices and the free-migration sales promises that identify the first 10 customers by name.
Sharpening (6.6 to 7.2): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6 before). Original shape was "AI data migration for SaaS onboarding", which runs straight into Flatfile/OneSchema/Osmos/Dromo and Zengines. Change: moved the wedge off clean-file mapping (crowded, embeddable importers own it) to the two steps nobody packages — (a) sources that are PDF/printed reports with undocumented codes, (b) the reconciliation + customer sign-off pack. Research found: switching guides explicitly flag "we give you a PDF" as the failure case and document per-record-only document retrieval (dentalpin, wemigrate); Reducto/Extend sell parsing components but have no report discovery, cross-report reconciliation or import connectors; reconciliation tooling exists (QuerySurge, AWS DMS validation, Syntra DataVault) but aimed at data engineers, with the summary concluding the end-to-end business-readable proof-of-completion workflow for implementation teams is the standing gap. Gap 6 → 7 (not 8: Zengines explicitly markets customer onboarding for software companies, and Rocketlane's Migration Agent has sign-off, so the gap is packaging and price point, not absence).

Round 2 — weak criterion: market_pull (6 before). Original buyer was "SaaS implementation teams" generically, which has no proven budget line. Change: narrowed to vendors who have already put a *price* on this work or who publicly absorb it. Research found published retail conversion prices (Open Dental $1,450/database + $850 docs + $900 X-rays; IDEXX Neo $590), consultant quotes of $6.5k-$15k standard and $18k-$40k complex, free-migration sales promises from NaVetor, Digitail, Vagaro, Ascora, Intellident, and live job postings for the manual role (Practice Migration Specialist $50-70k; Data Conversion Specialist $75-125k; Senior Data Conversion Engineer $105-130k). That is a named role with a confirmed budget and prices I can point at. Market_pull 6 → 7 (not 8-9: every one of those prices is charged *to the practice* by the vendor; I found no evidence of a vendor paying a third party for conversion software, so willingness to pay at the vendor level is inferred, not observed).

Wedge stayed 6 and I did not lift it: the honest first version needs a source-recipe abstraction, a review UI, API loaders and a reconciliation engine, and the first five conversions will be forward-deployed by hand. That is months, not weeks, and it is the main thing holding this to a 7.2 rather than an 8.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Apple container 1.7.1 cluster docs (confirmed local Kubernetes on macOS, Nov 6 2026 — real but needs a daemon, killed candidate 3), the x.ai Grok Bot accounting post (confirmed the five named bot roles and the "structure the process first" lesson — but it mapped straight onto past ideas Roster/Payslip, so it was dropped as a repeat), and Claude Meetings (confirmed no public artifact API, killed candidate 7). Screening pot (5/5): geofencing in browsers (W3C issue 214 — no background geofences, killed Laundrygeo); local Kubernetes visualisers (Podman Desktop, Rancher, ClusterDeck already exist, killed Clusterboard); remote agent orchestrators (Symphony, Open SWE, Cezar — crowded, killed Agentswitchboard); AGENTS.md linters (found agentlinter and SkillCheck — narrowed Houserules away from being a plain linter); untangle-codebase (confirmed it's a Claude skill, cloning it was off the table). Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed the arXiv configuration-smells taxonomy and its public Zenodo replication package; confirmed the se-uhd dataset (4,738 repos, 18,167 config files, CC BY 4.0, downloadable, browsable site updated Oct 17 2026); confirmed the HuggingFace census dataset (8,390 file texts, published 22 Oct 2026, ~32MB, per-row licences incl. NOASSERTION — which forced the build plan to ship aggregates not bulk text); confirmed the census findings (26.3% adoption, 59.6% among top-starred, median 818 words, verify-before-done 49.7%, tests 48.2%, 74.0% of directives give no reason) that the headline output depends on; plus searches for an existing "compare your AGENTS.md to a corpus" tool that found none. Sharpening pot (2/4): confirmed ossrules.md is browse-and-curate only with no paste-and-score, and that ghostrules is a security auditor — which is what let me raise wow and usefulness honestly. Two sharpening calls unused; the remaining uncertainty (will people actually return weekly?) is behavioural and no search would settle it, which is why usefulness stayed at 7.
Sharpening (7.4 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6 before). The v1 was a one-shot score: paste, read, leave. Change to the idea: make the corpus the product, not the verdict — add a "rule of the week" surfaced from the census each Monday (a real rule from a named repo, with its prevalence), and store the last score in localStorage so a re-scan shows the delta after you edit your file. Research: checked whether a corpus-backed, recurring reference already exists — ossrules.md (confirmed via summary) is a curated 100-project browsable library with side-by-side compare, but explicitly does not score your pasted file and has no recurring hook; agentlinter has rules but no corpus; SkillCheck validates schemas. Nothing well-known does the recurring corpus-vs-you loop. Usefulness 6 → 7 (capped: a weekly hook is plausible but unproven, and an AGENTS.md is edited monthly, not daily). Round 2 — weak criterion: wow (7 before). Change: lead the output not with a score but with the single most damning line — "X% of popular repos tell their agent to verify before declaring done. Yours doesn't." — backed by the census's measured per-rule prevalence (verify-before-done 49.7%, write tests 48.2%, rules about the instruction files themselves 44.3%, median 818 words, 74.0% of directives give no reason), each with a real example file. Research: confirmed those specific numbers exist in the Oct 2026 census (arXiv 2610.31715) and that the underlying 8,390-file corpus is downloadable from HuggingFace, so the headline claim is checkable rather than invented. Wow 7 → 8. Shareability held at 8 (the card is personal to your repo and the format is proven to spread, but no comparable corpus-card has actually gone viral that I could verify). Average 7.4 → 7.8.
prototype_summary: A clickable prototype showing a dental practice's unreadable legacy PDFs turning into a mapped, exception-resolved, signed-off conversion reconciliation pack in three steps.
